primary_source.title: Mimalloc: Free List Sharding in Action

machines.authority: prose in sections 4.3 and 4.4, not the strings embedded in the figures

figure_label_conflicts.where: Figure 3 embedded label, and the same string repeats on the SpecMark and Xeon RSS figures
figure_label_conflicts.label: HP-Z4-G4, 16Gb; 8-core Intel XEON @2.7Ghz; Ubuntu 18.04.1, GCC 7.4.0
figure_label_conflicts.conflicts_with: section 4.4 prose: 4-core W-2123 at 3.6 GHz, GCC 7.3.0
figure_label_conflicts.resolution: Exact comparisons use the prose. The figure label is recorded so it is not silently treated as a second official machine.

paper_measurement.note: The project round-1 protocol still uses 3 warmup + 15 measured runs and perf counters. That is the project's acceptance procedure. It is not a claim that the paper did this.

paper_thread_policy.suffix_N: benchmarks whose name ends in N run on all cores of that machine
paper_thread_policy.larsonN: the workload itself uses 100 threads, independent of the machine core count
paper_thread_policy.alloc_testN: N cores, 100e6 allocations per thread, objects up to 1 KiB

allocators.identity: debian source package, not a raw git checkout

upstream_tag_not_identical.why_not_the_pin: The Ubuntu revision adds Debian patches. The paper names the package.

allocators.paper: secure mimalloc, same tag as mi, secure build

workloads.paper: Redis 5.0.3, 1 million requests, push 10 list elements then read the head 10
workloads.build_note: mimalloc-bench builds it with USE_JEMALLOC=no MALLOC=libc, then LD_PRELOADs the allocator under test

workloads.paper: 100 threads, some objects freed by other threads
updated sources from the SuperMalloc repository; 100 allocating and 100 deallocating threads

workloads.resolved_via: leanprover/lean now serves this object through the lean4 repository; the commit message is the 3.4.1 release

workloads.paper: Hoard cache-scratch; section 4.3 reports mimalloc more than 18x faster than jemalloc and tcmalloc. That multiple is not an Exact target.

bench_suite.why_this_commit: README text matches paper section 4, and build-bench-env.sh still installs tcmalloc from the Ubuntu package named in the paper.

script_does_not_check_out_mimalloc_tag.what_the_script_does: git clone https://github.com/daanx/mimalloc && git checkout dev
script_does_not_check_out_mimalloc_tag.why: The tag object is dated 2019-07-09, after this suite commit. The paper names the tag. The branch tip is not the pin.

rejected_later_pins.what: build-bench-env.sh checks out gperftools tag gperftools-2.7 (commit 9608fa3bcf8020d35f59fbf70cd3cbe4b015b972) and comments out libgoogle-perftools-dev
rejected_later_pins.why_rejected: The paper and the README still say Ubuntu package 2.5-2.2ubuntu3. Using 2.7 would be a different replication.

closes.C1: yes, on alloc-test, larson, xmalloc, redis only
closes.C2: directional yes inside the 1..12 sweep; the published 100-thread point is extra
closes.scalability: yes only if the host has at least 12 hardware threads
closes.C5: yes, RSS of those four workloads only
closes.C3: partial: perf counters on those workloads; the mechanism still needs the locality result and ablation

preflight.reason: A 6/8/12-thread point on fewer hardware threads measures oversubscription, not allocator scaling.

checked_facts_that_are_not_round_1_targe.fact: A bump-pointer variant was consistently about 2% slower across the paper's benchmarks, attributed to a second conditional on the fast path.
checked_facts_that_are_not_round_1_targe.not_a_target_because: Round-1 does not build that variant. The isolated harness result (bump faster on an L1-resident loop) is a different experiment.
